item.title: Tokushima Events 2026: Awa Odori, Fireworks & Machi Asobi
item.description: Tokushima’s event calendar is defined by one of the most electrifying festivals on earth. For four August nights, the whole city of Tokushima becomes a stage for the Awa Odori — 400 years of dance, drums, and the cry of “fools dancing, fools watching, so dance!” Around it, the prefecture offers the roaring Naruto whirlpools at their spring peak, a twice-yearly anime festival that takes over the city, and the deep-mountain quiet of the Iya Valley.

item.title: Awa Odori Dance Lesson: Learn the Steps — Guide
item.description: You don’t need to come during the August festival to experience Awa Odori — at the Awa Odori Kaikan in Tokushima city, the dance is celebrated all year round. The hall stages regular live performances by professional ‘ren’ dance troupes, who demonstrate the men’s dynamic low crouch and the women’s elegant, poised style to live drums and shamisen. Best of all, at the end audience members are invited up to learn and try the steps themselves in a fun, hands-on lesson, guided by the dancers — a great way to feel the rhythm and joy of Awa Odori firsthand.

item.title: Awa Odori: Japan's Greatest Dance Festival — Guide
item.description: Awa Odori is the most famous dance festival in Japan and the pride of Tokushima, held each year during the mid-August Obon season and drawing well over a million spectators. Over four days and nights, the streets of Tokushima city fill with ‘ren’ — dance troupes of choreographed performers, some over a hundred strong — parading and dancing to the driving, hypnotic rhythm of taiko drums, shamisen, flutes and bells. The dance has a distinctive loose, flowing style, with dancers in colourful yukata and the women in half-moon straw hats, all chanting the famous refrain: ‘the dancing fool and the watching fool are both fools, so you might as well dance!

item.title: Koenji Awa Odori Guide: Tokyo's Biggest Summer Dance Festival
item.description: For two evenings every August, the laid-back western Tokyo neighbourhood of Koenji erupts into the city’s largest and most exhilarating dance festival. Some 10,000 dancers in traditional costume pour through the streets to the hypnotic, driving rhythm of shamisen, taiko drums, and flutes, while up to a million spectators line the route. This is the Koenji Awa Odori — the biggest awa odori celebration outside its birthplace in Tokushima, and one of the great experiences of a Tokyo summer.
